title: When the sculpture garden floods: front‑desk printed step‑free indoor route (with desk sign)
description: A short visitor notice limited to on‑site distribution: a free printed indoor route available at the front desk (and a small sign placed by the desk) that tells visitors the route starts at the front desk, follows step‑free public corridors through the permanent sculpture galleries, and ends at the café. The copy will tell visitors to check the same‑day garden notice before travelling and clarify that this is a temporary alternative, not a permanent replacement for the garden. (Optional next step, not documented in the source: propose adding this notice to the website or phone scripts for days the garden is closed.)
audience: On‑site visitors who had planned to visit the sculpture garden and who arrive at or speak with the front desk.
rationale: The source frames the item as a visitor note intended to help visitors adapt when the garden is closed. The printed handout and small desk sign match what was used in the April pilot. The notice is intended to reduce visitor confusion about what to do when the garden is closed (the pilot recorded some visitors asking where to start), while making clear accessibility (step‑free), the start/end points, and that the indoor route is not a permanent replacement. The museum did not collect systematic data on route completion or visitor satisfaction during the pilot, so any claim of measured benefit would be unsupported by the source.
evidence: Source: “the front desk can give visitors a free printed route”; “The route starts at the front desk and ends at the café”; “It follows step‑free public corridors”; “Visitors should still check the same‑day garden notice before travelling.” Pilot: “In April, the museum handed out the route at two wet Sunday openings. The desk counted 38 copies handed out. At the first opening some visitors asked where to start, so a sign was added by the desk at the second.” Limits: “Staff recorded no systematic counts of how many visitors completed the route and did not track visitor satisfaction.” Also: “The note is intended to help visitors adapt their visit when the garden is closed. There is no plan to replace the garden visit permanently.”

title: Front‑desk briefing and desk sign template for distributing the route
description: A short internal guidance sheet and printable desk sign: what to say when offering the printed route (start point, step‑free corridor, end at café, check same‑day garden notice), when to offer it, and a standard small sign template for placement by the front desk (reflecting the pilot addition of a desk sign).
audience: Front‑of‑house staff and volunteers who will distribute the printed route and answer visitor questions at the desk.
rationale: The pilot recorded 38 handouts over two openings and noted visitors asked where to start; a standardized script and desk sign can ensure consistent information is given to visitors arriving at the desk. The source does not report measured changes in visitor understanding, so guidance should be framed as a practical consistency measure rather than proven improvement.
evidence: Source: desk gave out printed routes in April (38 copies over two wet Sunday openings); “At the first opening some visitors asked where to start, so a sign was added by the desk at the second.” The route’s details (start, step‑free corridors, end at café) are documented in the source.

title: Internal pilot summary noting data gaps and suggested next evaluation steps
description: A brief management memo summarising the April pilot distribution (two wet Sundays, 38 copies handed out; desk sign added after initial questions), the limits of the pilot (no counts of completion, no visitor satisfaction data), and recommended next steps if management wants evidence before any scaling (e.g., simple completion counts, brief exit question on satisfaction, or repeat on more closed‑garden days).
audience: Museum management and program leads deciding whether to formalise or evaluate the indoor route.
rationale: The source records what was done and explicitly documents missing measurements; management needs that context to decide whether to resource, evaluate or expand the alternative. The memo should recommend lightweight evaluation measures because the pilot did not collect them.
evidence: Source: “In April, the museum handed out the route at two wet Sunday openings. The desk counted 38 copies handed out.” Limits: “Staff recorded no systematic counts of how many visitors completed the route and did not track visitor satisfaction.” Also: “The note is intended to help visitors adapt their visit when the garden is closed. There is no plan to replace the garden visit permanently.”

title: Accessibility note for visitors who need step‑free access
description: A concise on‑site statement for use at the desk (and in any printed material) emphasising that the indoor route follows step‑free public corridors and is available free at the front desk when the sculpture garden is closed. Remind readers to check the same‑day garden notice and that this is an alternative for closed‑garden days only.
audience: Visitors with mobility needs, carers, and accessibility advisors checking on‑site information at the front desk.
rationale: The source explicitly states the route follows step‑free public corridors; making that information prominent at the desk helps mobility‑restricted visitors plan their visit. The source does not document outreach beyond on‑site distribution, so the note should be limited to in‑person availability and the same‑day notice reminder.
evidence: Source: “It follows step‑free public corridors”; “the front desk can give visitors a free printed route”; “Visitors should still check the same‑day garden notice before travelling.”

title: Suggested web/phone notification (proposal, not in source): ‘Garden closed today? Pick up an indoor route at the front desk’
description: A draft short web/social/phone script to be used on days the garden is closed, directing visitors to pick up the free printed route at the front desk, noting the route is step‑free and ends at the café, and linking to or offering the printable PDF if the museum chooses to publish it online. Clearly label this as a proposed extension of the pilot rather than an existing practice documented in the source.
audience: Communications staff who may choose to extend the on‑site handout to online and phone channels.
rationale: The source documents only on‑site printed distribution and a desk sign. If the museum wants to reduce travel disruption further, communications could optionally publish the route or include it in phone scripts; this idea is an editorial recommendation and is not claimed to be already implemented in the source.
evidence: Source documents on‑site practice: printed route available at front desk and a small desk sign was added after the pilot. The source does not state the route was published online or promoted by phone; this idea is a proposed next step rather than current practice.
